title: ASMOS
summary: ASMOS, also described by Deepak as an Adaptive Semantic Memory Operating System, is his flagship multi-agent memory project. It is a research-grade working prototype, not just a paper idea: Deepak reports code for routing, scoring, and memory; 400+ passing tests; Docker support; and experiments on Stack Overflow Q&A data with real AI models. ASMOS uses verified checkpoints to identify topic owners and load only the relevant memory slice. The final re-test showed about 22% token reduction, with results roughly in the 18-26% range depending on the question.

title: ASMOS evaluation
summary: Deepak evaluated ASMOS by comparing the actual prompt text sent to AI models in two modes: a baseline that loads broad memory and an ASMOS mode that loads only the owner agent's relevant memory. Tokens were counted with a real tokenizer across 50 questions and 10 random-seed reruns, then checked for statistical significance. The final result is about 22% token reduction, with an observed range around 18-26%.

title: ASMOS ownership scoring
summary: ASMOS chooses a topic owner with a weighted score: 60% trust, based on how often an agent's past answers were verified correct, and 40% contribution share, based on what fraction of correct answers on that topic came from that agent. New agents begin with a modest default trust score so they are not locked out. If nobody stands out clearly enough, ASMOS falls back to broader memory search instead of forcing a close guess.

title: Turb-DETR — verified detail
summary: Turb-DETR is a five-person PES University team project. A direct code audit found 32 commits, of which Deepak authored 15 and a teammate 16, and 14 real pytest tests covering data-split integrity, the turbidity augmentation's output shape and reproducibility, and the SimAM module's gradient flow and zero parameter count. The technical core is SimAM, a parameter-free attention module from a cited ICML 2021 paper, injected between the CNN and Transformer stages of RT-DETR so backscatter noise is suppressed before self-attention can spread it, paired with a physically-grounded Jaffe-McGlamery turbidity simulation rather than a generic blur. Honest status: the experimental plan is thorough but no benchmark results are committed yet — the results and paper directories contain only placeholders.

title: ShortcutScore — verified detail
summary: ShortcutScore is a three-person project where Deepak holds the largest commit share, 14 of 23. It builds a single scalar metric from three interpretability signals — attribution-outside-object ratio, attribution bias index, and counterfactual sensitivity — to quantify when an image classifier is relying on spurious background cues rather than the object itself. It was validated on the Waterbirds benchmark and a synthetic CIFAR-10 bias-injection test. A real ablation file in the repo records Cohen's d of 0.383, AUROC of 0.602 and p of 0.040 over 50 images: a genuine but modest effect, reported as such. Note the repo is named 'tdl-project' on GitHub even though the project is called ShortcutScore.

title: The experiment that failed first
summary: In ShortcutScore, the synthetic monotonicity experiment injected a visible watermark into CIFAR-10 images to check that the score rose as bias strength increased. The first version used a 4x4 patch and failed outright, because Grad-CAM's spatial resolution could not reliably localise attribution to a region that small. The corrected setup used an 8x8 patch. Deepak documented the failure and the fix in the project README rather than quietly removing it, and the lesson generalises: attribution-based metrics need a shortcut region large enough for the attribution method's resolution.

title: Smart Door Lock

Deepak wrote every one of the 16 commits, including a custom Express server that bridges serial data from an Arduino Mega to the ESP32-CAM over WebSocket and REST, plus a React and Tailwind frontend; two teammates are credited in the README for hardware work that does not appear in git. Built March to May 2025. Honest scope: it is a hardware demo, and the only test file is the untouched Create React App default, so the authentication logic has no automated coverage.
